heroIntro: Following the tragic demise of a parent, families face immense emotional grief alongside sudden administrative hurdles. When heirs approach the deceased's bank branch to access savings accounts, Fixed Deposit Receipts (FDR), or treasury bonds, they are frequently met with bureaucratic resistance: bank managers refuse withdrawals, citing outdated regulations, or an estranged sibling nominated on the account claims absolute personal ownership of all funds to the exclusion of other heirs. In Bangladesh, banking operations and inheritance laws are strictly regulated. The Supreme Court has unequivocally established that a nominee is merely a trustee/custodian—not the beneficial owner. Understanding how to navigate Bangladesh Bank regulations and obtain a Succession Certificate from the Joint District Judge Court under the Succession Act 1925 is the definitive legal key to releasing and distributing your rightful family inheritance.

quickAnswer.title: Quick Answer: How Do Legal Heirs Claim a Deceased Parent's Bank Account and FDR in Bangladesh?
quickAnswer.text: Under the landmark rulings of the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh and Bangladesh Bank Master Circulars, a bank nominee is merely a custodian authorized to receive funds on behalf of all legal heirs; the nominee does not become the beneficial owner. The money belongs entirely to the legal heirs according to Muslim or Hindu personal inheritance laws. For small balances, banks may disburse funds upon submission of a Warishan Certificate, death certificate, and an indemnity bond. For substantial bank balances, Fixed Deposit Receipts (FDR), or where disputes arise among heirs, the bank will freeze withdrawals until the legal heirs obtain a Succession Certificate from the Court of the Joint District Judge under Section 372 of the Succession Act 1925.
highlights: The Supreme Court has confirmed that a bank account nominee is only a trustee and cannot withhold funds from other legal heirs.
All bank balances, FDRs, and prize bonds must be distributed strictly according to personal laws of succession (Faraiz).
Banks require an official Succession Certificate from the Joint District Judge Court for large deposits or disputed accounts.
Court fees for a Succession Certificate are statutory and capped, ensuring heirs can access substantial estates affordably.

Step 2: Collect bank account numbers, FDR receipts, and balance confirmation certificates from the relevant bank branches.
Step 3: If the nominee attempts to misappropriate funds, serve an immediate legal notice on the bank branch manager to freeze withdrawals.
Step 4: File a Succession Case under Section 372 of the Succession Act 1925 before the Joint District Judge Court.

sections.title: The Challenge: Accessing Deceased Parents' Bank Accounts
sections.content:
When a parent passes away in Bangladesh, their estate consists not only of immovable lands and homesteads, but frequently of substantial liquid assets: savings accounts, Fixed Deposit Receipts (FDR), current corporate accounts, national savings certificates (Sanchayapatra), and locker contents. Heirs expect that by presenting the deceased's death certificate and the local Chairman's Warishan Certificate (heirship certificate), the bank will promptly divide and disburse the money.

In reality, bank compliance procedures are stringent. Commercial banks fear wrongful disbursement liability and conflicting claims among family members. Under Section 103 of the Bank Company Act 1991, banks operate with immense caution. If the deceased parent did not name a nominee, named an estranged relative who refuses to share, or left a multi-lakh FDR deposit, bank managers immediately freeze operations and issue a formal compliance letter: 'Please obtain and submit a Succession Certificate from the competent civil court.' Understanding the legal pathway to procure this certificate is essential to prevent family assets from languishing indefinitely in frozen bank vaults.

sections.title: Nominee vs. Legal Heirs: The Supreme Court Settled Law
sections.content:
For decades, a bitter legal controversy raged in Bangladesh: does the nominee named in a bank account form become the absolute owner of the money upon the depositor's death, or are they merely an agent receiving the money for all legal heirs? Selfish nominees routinely argued that Section 103 of the Bank Company Act 1991 gave them exclusive rights, cutting out daughters, elderly mothers, or younger siblings.

This dispute was decisively and permanently settled by the Supreme Court of Bangladesh. In landmark judgments of both the High Court Division and the Appellate Division (including the celebrated Bangladesh Bank vs. Bilkis Hossain jurisprudence), the highest court established that a nominee is merely a collector or trustee. The court ruled that nomination does not constitute a gift (Hiba) or a will (Wasiyat). The nominee's sole function is to receive the funds from the bank to give the bank a valid discharge of liability; once received, the money forms part of the deceased's general estate and must be distributed among all statutory heirs strictly according to their religious personal law (Faraiz under Islamic law or Hindu succession rules). Any nominee who appropriates the funds solely for themselves commits criminal breach of trust under Section 406 of the Penal Code 1860.

sections.title: Bangladesh Bank Regulations on Deceased Depositors
sections.content:
The central bank, Bangladesh Bank, has issued detailed Master Circulars to commercial banks regarding the treatment of deceased depositors' accounts. These regulations balance administrative convenience with heirship protection:

  • Small Balance Protocol (Without Court Certificate): For relatively minor balances (typically amounts under BDT 1,00,000 to BDT 2,00,000, depending on the internal policy of the bank), banks can release funds without a Succession Certificate if all legal heirs appear in person, execute a joint indemnity bond, and submit certified death certificates and Warishan certificates.
  • Substantial Balances & FDRs: Where the balance is substantial (exceeding bank policy thresholds, or involving large term deposits/FDRs), banks are legally mandated to demand an authenticated Succession Certificate issued by the Joint District Judge Court.
  • Disputed Accounts: If any single heir submits a written objection claiming that the nominee is acting fraudulently or that certain heirs are being concealed, the bank must instantaneously place a 'Debit Block' on the account, disallowing any withdrawals until a court order is produced.

Understanding these thresholds prevents heirs from wasting months arguing with branch officers when a civil court petition is the mandatory legal requirement.

sections.title: What Is a Succession Certificate Under the 1925 Act?
sections.content:
A Succession Certificate is a specialized judicial document granted by a civil court under Part X (Sections 370 to 390) of the Succession Act 1925. It provides official judicial authority to the person(s) named therein to collect debts and securities due to the estate of a deceased individual and to give valid discharge to debtors, including commercial banks, insurance companies, and public institutions.

It is important to distinguish a Succession Certificate from a Letters of Administration or Probate: a Succession Certificate applies exclusively to 'debts and securities'—meaning liquid cash in bank accounts, FDRs, shares, bonds, mutual funds, and government savings certificates. It does not apply to immovable agricultural lands or residential buildings. Once the court grants the certificate, commercial banks are statutorily bound to disburse the specified amounts according to the percentage shares specified in the court's decree.

sections.title: Step-by-Step Procedure in the Joint District Judge Court
sections.content:
Procuring a Succession Certificate requires a structured judicial procedure before the Court of the Joint District Judge within whose territorial jurisdiction the deceased ordinarily resided or where the bank branch is situated:

  1. Drafting the Petition (Section 372 Succession Act): The petition must specify the exact date and place of death, annex the official death certificate, list all surviving legal heirs with their relationship and ages, provide the Faraiz calculation of shares, and detail the exact bank accounts, FDR numbers, and monetary sums.
  2. Filing and Gazetted Newspaper Notice: Upon admission of the petition, the court orders a public citation published in a widely circulated national Bengali daily newspaper, providing 15 to 30 days for any potential claimant or creditor to file an objection.
  3. Ex Parte Hearing or Contested Evidence: If no objections are filed, the petitioner appears before the judge, submits original documents (FDR receipts, death certificates, Warishan Sanad), and tenders formal oral evidence confirming the family pedigree.
  4. Judicial Grant and Security Bond: The court passes an order granting the Succession Certificate. Upon furnishing the requisite court fees and any indemnity bond required by the court, the official sealed certificate is signed and issued.

Typically, an uncontested Succession Case concludes within 60 to 90 days when handled by experienced banking and succession counsel.

sections.title: Court Fees and Statutory Costs for Succession Certificates
sections.content:
A common apprehension among heirs is that court fees for releasing bank funds will consume their inheritance. In Bangladesh, court fees for a Succession Certificate are governed by the Court-fees Act 1870 (Schedule I, Article 12) and Ministry of Law statutory notifications.

Under current statutory rates, the ad-valorem court fee is calculated as a small percentage of the total debt/security value, subject to a statutory maximum cap. For modest sums, the court fee is minimal; for multi-million-taka estates, the fee is legally capped to prevent disproportionate burden on grieving families. When weighed against the prospect of leaving tens of lakhs of taka frozen indefinitely or losing the funds entirely to a rogue nominee, statutory court costs represent a modest, structured investment to secure permanent, unchallengeable legal ownership.

sections.title: How to Freeze an Account If a Nominee Tries to Flee
sections.content:
In crisis situations, heirs discover that an untrustworthy sibling or relative named as nominee is quietly communicating with the bank branch manager to withdraw the entire FDR balance and transfer it to their personal account. If the funds are cashed out and converted into cash, recovering them through years of civil litigation is exceptionally difficult.

To prevent immediate asset flight, legal counsel executes an emergency two-step intervention:

  • Immediate Advocate Notice to Branch Manager: Dispatch an urgent formal legal notice to the bank branch manager, regional head, and managing director, citing the Appellate Division ruling on nominee trusteeship. The notice informs the bank that the depositor has deceased, lists the legal heirs, asserts an active dispute, and warns that if the bank disburses funds solely to the nominee, the bank officers will be held personally liable for aiding criminal breach of trust. Upon receiving this notice, banks immediately freeze withdrawals to protect themselves from liability.
  • Injunction from Civil Court: Concurrently, file an application before the Joint District Judge or Family Court for an interim order of injunction restraining the bank from disbursing funds until the disposal of the Succession Case.

This swift action locks the money safely inside the banking system until the court determines each heir's lawful percentage.

sections.title: Illustrative Scenario: Recovering an FDR from a Hostile Nominee
sections.content:
The following illustrative scenario (composite; names and details changed) demonstrates how siblings protected their inheritance from a rogue nominee in Dhaka:

A retired government physician passed away in Dhanmondi, leaving behind three children: two married daughters living abroad in London and an unmarried son living with him. The father held BDT 65,00,000 across two Fixed Deposit Receipts (FDR) in a private commercial bank. Unbeknownst to his sisters, the son had persuaded his ailing father to nominate him as the sole nominee on both FDR accounts. Following the father's demise, the son visited the bank, presented the death certificate, and requested the entire BDT 65,00,000 be transferred into his personal account, falsely informing the branch manager that he was the only surviving child.

When the daughters discovered the deception, they contacted an advocate in Dhaka. The advocate immediately drafted an emergency legal notice served by hand to the branch manager and the bank's head of legal. The notice attached the registered Nikahnama, the family's official Warishan Sanad issued by Dhaka South City Corporation proving the existence of the two daughters, and cited Supreme Court rulings establishing that the nominee is strictly a trustee. Fearing legal liability, the bank placed an immediate freeze on both FDRs.

The advocate then filed a Succession Case in the Court of the Joint District Judge, Dhaka, on behalf of the daughters. The court issued public citations and summoned the bank's account statements. During the hearing, the son's lawyer conceded that under Islamic Faraiz law, the son was entitled to 50% of the estate, while each daughter was entitled to 25%. The Joint District Judge issued a Succession Certificate distributing the BDT 65,00,000 strictly according to the statutory Faraiz shares. The bank disbursed the funds via three separate certified pay orders, ensuring justice and preserving the daughters' lawful inheritance.

faqs.question: Does a nominee own the bank money after the account holder dies in Bangladesh?
faqs.answer: No. The Supreme Court of Bangladesh has firmly settled that a nominee is merely a trustee and custodian. The money belongs to all legal heirs according to their personal inheritance laws (Faraiz), and the nominee must distribute the funds among all statutory heirs.

faqs.question: What is a Succession Certificate and why does the bank demand it?
faqs.answer: A Succession Certificate is a court order issued by the Joint District Judge Court under the Succession Act 1925 empowering legal heirs to collect debts and securities of a deceased person. Banks require it for large deposits or disputed accounts to protect themselves from wrongful disbursement claims.

faqs.question: How long does it take to get a Succession Certificate in Bangladesh?
faqs.answer: An uncontested Succession Case typically takes between 60 to 90 days from filing to certificate issuance, which includes the mandatory 15-30 day public newspaper citation period.

faqs.question: Can an FDR be cashed out without a Succession Certificate?
faqs.answer: For smaller sums, some banks may release funds upon submission of a certified Warishan Certificate, death certificate, and an indemnity bond signed by all legal heirs. For substantial FDR amounts, a court Succession Certificate is mandatory.

faqs.question: What should I do if a nominee is secretly trying to withdraw all the money?
faqs.answer: Immediately serve a formal Advocate Legal Notice on the bank branch manager and regional office, informing them of the death and the legal heirs. The bank will place an immediate 'Debit Block' on the account to freeze withdrawals.

faqs.question: What documents are required to file a Succession Case in Bangladesh?
faqs.answer: You need the official Death Certificate, Chairman/Councillor Warishan Certificate, National ID copies of all heirs, bank statements or FDR certificates with exact account numbers, and the calculated Faraiz distribution shares.

faqs.question: Can overseas Bangladeshi heirs (NRB) claim bank money without traveling to Bangladesh?
faqs.answer: Yes. An NRB heir can execute a Special Power of Attorney attested by the local Bangladesh Embassy or High Commission abroad, appointing a trusted representative or lawyer in Bangladesh to file the Succession Case and collect their share.

faqs.question: What happens if the nominee spends the money and refuses to share with other heirs?
faqs.answer: The nominee commits criminal breach of trust under Section 406 of the Penal Code 1860, punishable by up to 3 years imprisonment. The legal heirs can file a criminal case in the Magistrate Court and a civil suit for recovery and asset attachment.
